title: can, could, may: ability, requests and permission
tagline: Three small words for what you can do, and for asking politely.
why: Can I…? Could you…? May I…? These are some of the most useful questions in English — for permission, for polite requests, and for saying what you're able to do. Speaking Part 1 often asks What can you do?, and Reading Part 1 signs use can't and may not for rules. Choosing between can, could and may is really about how polite you need to be.

hook.text: In Trujillo, Liam wants to try his cousin's skateboard. "Can I try it?" he asks. "Could you wear a helmet first?" says his aunt. "Of course! I can't skate without one anyway," laughs Liam. "May I watch?" asks Nadia.
hook.ask: Three little words — can, could and may — all do a similar job here. Can you find them and say what each one is asking for?

use.point: Can I…? / Could I…? / May I…? — asking for permission

examples.note: can I = the everyday way to ask
may I = the most polite, formal way to ask

use.point: Can you…? / Could you…? — polite requests, and be able to

examples.note: could you = a polite request to someone else

examples.text: Can you help me with this bag?
I'll be able to skate better after more practice.
examples.note: be able to for the future — will can't be followed by can

watch_out.why: Can/could/may go straight before the base verb — no to.
Modal verbs never add -s, even for he/she/it.

watch_out.wrong: I will can skate better soon.
watch_out.right: I'll be able to skate better soon.
watch_out.why: You can't put two modals together — use be able to after will.

watch_out.wrong: Can I to borrow your pen?
watch_out.why: No to after can, even in a question.
The short answer stops at the modal — don't add do.

l1.wrong: I can to swim very well.
l1.why: The Spanish 'puedo + infinitivo' tempts you to add to — English can never takes to.
The base verb comes straight after can, with no to, even in questions.

l1.es: Sabía nadar cuando tenía seis años.
l1.wrong: I knew swim when I had six years.
l1.right: I could swim when I was six.
l1.why: Past ability in English uses could, not a word-for-word translation of sabía — and age uses was, not had.
A polite request in English starts with Could you…?, not a plain statement turned into a question.

remember.trick: can = now, could = past or polite, may = most polite.
remember.tip: Think of a politeness ladder: can is the everyday step, could is one step up, and may is right at the top.

can_do: I can say what I can and can't do, now and in the past, with can and could.
I can ask for permission politely with Can I…?, Could I…? and May I…?.
I can make polite requests with Can you…? and Could you…?.
summary: Can/can't = ability now; could/couldn't = ability in the past.
Can I…?, Could I…? and May I…? all ask for permission — may is the most polite.
Can you…? and Could you…? ask someone else to do something for you.
The base verb comes straight after can/could/may — no to, and no -s, even for he/she/it.
For the future, or after another modal, use be able to — you can't say 'will can'.
